propositions.text: The Administrator seeks summary judgment against Dodds under the Federal Courts Rules.
propositions.quote: The Administrator (the “Administrator”) of the Ship Source Oil Pollution Fund (the “Fund” or the “Plaintiff”) seeks summary judgment, pursuant to the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106 (the “Rules”), against Tracy Donald Dodds (the “Defendant”).

paragraphs.summary: The Administrator seeks summary judgment against Dodds under the Federal Courts Rules, says the court.

propositions.text: Plaintiff commenced action on October 4, 2016 seeking $382,353.33 plus interest and costs for pollution damage from the sinking of the Involved Ship.
propositions.quote: By statement of claim issued on October 4, 2016 the Plaintiff commenced an action against the Defendant seeking judgment in the amount of $382,353.33, together with interest at the Admiralty rate and costs.

propositions.text: Claim relates to costs of repairing and preventing pollution from sinking and oil discharge of the Involved Ship.
propositions.quote: The claim relates to the costs of repairing, remedying, minimizing and preventing pollution damage resulting from the sinking of and discharge of oil from the Ship “RYAN ATLANTIC II”, formerly named “CAPE ROUGE” (the “Involved Ship”).

paragraphs.summary: The Plaintiff commenced action on October 4, 2016 seeking $382,353.33 plus interest and costs for pollution damage from the sinking of the Involved Ship, says the court.

propositions.text: Plaintiff alleges the Involved Ship sank at Bridgewater, Nova Scotia between March 10 and 12, 2014, causing oil discharge and cleanup until about April 7, 2014.
propositions.quote: In the statement of claim the Plaintiff alleges that the Involved Ship sank at her berth at Bridgewater, Nova Scotia between March 10 and March 12, 2014. It alleges that oil was discharged as a result and that clean-up work and work to prevent further pollution was conducted until on or about April 7, 2014.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff alleges the Involved Ship sank at Bridgewater, Nova Scotia between March 10 and 12, 2014, causing oil discharge and cleanup until about April 7, 2014, says the court.

propositions.text: Statement of Claim describes Defendant as registered owner of the Involved Ship.
propositions.quote: The Statement of Claim describes the Defendant as a “registered owner” of the Involved Ship.

paragraphs.summary: Statement of Claim describes Defendant as registered owner of the Involved Ship, says the court.

propositions.text: Defendant denies ownership and involvement with the vessel after January 2010, claiming sale to Earl Bisson on January 25, 2010 with proof of payment.
propositions.quote: 4. The defendant states the allegation in paragraph 3 and 10 is untrue as the defendant did not own the vessel Ryan Atlantic II upon payment on the 25 January 2010, and did not participate in any involvement with the vessel after the 30 January 2010. The vessel was sold to Earl Bisson Enfield N S [sic] 25 January 2010 and he was in possession immediately. The defendant has proof of payment from the lawyers trust account by way of bank drafts as per the purchasers [sic] request.

paragraphs.summary: Defendant denies ownership and involvement after January 2010, claiming sale to Earl Bisson with proof of payment, says the Defendant.

propositions.text: Plaintiff's motion record includes affidavit of Administrator Anne Legars with 23 exhibits detailing cleanup steps and invoices by Canadian Coast Guard.
propositions.quote: The motion record filed by the Plaintiff in support of the motion for summary judgment includes the affidavit of Anne Legars, currently the Administrator of the Fund, setting out the evidentiary basis of the Plaintiff’s claim. Her affidavit runs from page 3 to page 478 and includes 23 exhibits. The exhibits outline clean-up steps and related work undertaken by the Canadian Coast Guard (the “CCG”), as well as invoices related to the costs of those undertakings.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff's motion record includes affidavit of Administrator Anne Legars with 23 exhibits detailing cleanup steps and invoices by Canadian Coast Guard, says the court.

propositions.text: Plaintiff filed memorandum of fact and law citing Marine Liability Act and International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage, which has force of law in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff also filed a memorandum of fact and law, setting out its legal arguments with reference to the Marine Liability Act, S.C. 2001, c. 6 (the “Act”) and the International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage (the “BC”). The BC has the force of law in Canada pursuant to sections 69 and 70 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff filed memorandum citing Marine Liability Act and International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage, which has force of law in Canada, says the court.

propositions.text: Defendant participated in hearing and made oral submissions but filed no affidavit evidence.
propositions.quote: The Defendant participated in the hearing of the Plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment and made oral submissions. However, he did not file any evidence by way of affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: Defendant participated in hearing and made oral submissions but filed no affidavit evidence, says the court.

propositions.text: Plaintiff relies on Transport Canada ship registration website showing Defendant as owner despite spelling variations.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff relies on the information contained on the website for ship registration, maintained by the Department of Transport Canada, to plead that the Defendant is the owner of the Involved Ship. Two versions of the transcript are attached as exhibits to the affidavit of Ms. Legars, the first dated November 4, 2014 showing the owner to be “Tracey Donald Dobbs” and the second, dated December 1, 2016, showing the owner to be “Tracey Donald Dodds”.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff relies on Transport Canada ship registration website showing Defendant as owner despite spelling variations, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Plaintiff submits court should accept first record's spelling mistake and accept Defendant as registered owner due to same mailing address.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff submits that the Court should accept that the first record shows a spelling mistake and that the Court should accept that the Defendant is the registered owner since the mailing address is the same on each transcript.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff submits court should accept first record's spelling mistake and accept Defendant as registered owner due to same mailing address, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Plaintiff notes section 105 of Act authorizes Fund to pay reasonable cleanup costs and claims $382,353.33 plus interest and costs.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff notes that section 105 of the Act authorizes payment by the Fund of the “reasonable” costs of cleaning up oil pollution damage. It claims recovery of clean-up costs and related expenses in the amount of $382,353.33, together with interest at the Admiralty rate, pre-judgment interest, and costs.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff notes section 105 of Act authorizes Fund to pay reasonable cleanup costs and claims $382,353.33 plus interest and costs, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Administrator's affidavit states CCG accounts were carefully reviewed including by third party surveyor assessing reasonableness of charges.
propositions.quote: According to the affidavit of the Administrator, the accounts presented by the CCG were carefully reviewed, including a review by a third party, that is by Mr. M.J. Fegan, Surveyor to Fulcrum Marine Consultancy Ltd., engaged by the Fund to assess the reasonableness of the charges.

paragraphs.summary: Administrator's affidavit states CCG accounts were carefully reviewed including by third party surveyor assessing reasonableness of charges, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Payment by Fund gives rise to subrogated claim for recovery under subsection 106(3) of the Act.
propositions.quote: Payment of a claim by the Fund gives rise to a subrogated claim for recovery, pursuant to subsection 106(3) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Payment by Fund gives rise to subrogated claim for recovery under subsection 106(3) of the Act, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Administrator approved payment of $358,117.79 to CCG, offer accepted on April 24, 2015.
propositions.quote: The Administrator, by letter dated March 19, 2015, approved payment of the amount of $358,117.79 and offered to pay that amount to the CCG. By letter dated April 24, 2015, the offer was accepted.

paragraphs.summary: Administrator approved payment of $358,117.79 to CCG, offer accepted on April 24, 2015, says the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Defendant makes blanket denial of all allegations in statement of claim.
propositions.quote: In his Statement of Defence, the Defendant makes a blanket denial of all allegations in the statement of claim.

paragraphs.summary: Defendant makes blanket denial of all allegations in statement of claim, says the Defendant.

propositions.text: Defendant orally submits he sold the ship in 2010 to Mr. Bisson; sale unregistered due to Bisson's mistake completing documents.
propositions.quote: In his oral submissions made at the hearing of the motion, the Defendant said that he sold the Involved Ship in 2010 to a Mr. Bisson. He referred to a bill of sale and a bank draft. He said that the sale was not registered due to a mistake by Mr. Bisson in completing the documents.

paragraphs.summary: Defendant orally submits he sold the ship in 2010 to Mr. Bisson; sale unregistered due to Bisson's mistake completing documents, says the Defendant.

propositions.text: Court may grant summary judgment where there is no genuine issue for trial under Rule 215 of the Rules.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff seeks summary judgment. This Court may dispose of an action summarily where there is “no genuine issue for trial”, pursuant to Rule 215 of the Rules.

paragraphs.summary: Court may grant summary judgment where there is no genuine issue for trial under Rule 215 of the Rules, says the court.

propositions.text: Issue is whether there is a genuine issue for trial about Defendant's ownership status and liability for claimed amount.
propositions.quote: In this matter, the question is whether there is a genuine issue for trial relating the status of the Defendant as the “owner” of the Involved Ship and his liability for the amount claimed by the Plaintiff.

paragraphs.summary: Issue is whether there is a genuine issue for trial about Defendant's ownership status and liability for claimed amount, says the court.

propositions.text: Rule 214 requires response to summary judgment motion to set out specific facts and evidence showing genuine issue for trial, not relying on later evidence.
propositions.quote: A motion for summary judgment in the Federal Court is governed by Rules 213 to 218 of the Rules. Rule 214 is important and provides as follows: Summary Judgment Jugement sommaire Facts and evidence required Faits et éléments de preuve nécessaires 214 A response to a motion for summary judgment shall not rely on what might be adduced as evidence at a later stage in the proceedings. It must set out specific facts and adduce the evidence showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. 214 La réponse à une requête en jugement sommaire ne peut être fondée sur un élément qui pourrait être produit ultérieurement en preuve dans l’instance. Elle doit énoncer les faits précis et produire les éléments de preuve démontrant l’existence d’une véritable question litigieuse.

paragraphs.summary: Rule 214 requires response to summary judgment motion to set out specific facts and evidence showing genuine issue for trial, not relying on later evidence, says the court.

propositions.text: Rule 215(1) mandates summary judgment if no genuine issue for trial exists.
propositions.quote: Rule 215 spells out the circumstances when a motion for summary judgment will be granted and provides as follows : If no genuine issue for trial Absence de véritable question litigieuse 215 (1) If on a motion for summary judgment the Court is satisfied that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect to a claim or defence, the Court shall grant summary judgment accordingly.

propositions.text: Rule 215(2) allows trial or summary judgment with reference if only genuine issue is amount or question of law.
propositions.quote: (2) If the Court is satisfied that the only genuine issue is (2) Si la Cour est convaincue que la seule véritable question litigieuse est : (a) the amount to which the moving party is entitled, the Court may order a trial of that issue or grant summary judgment with a reference under rule 153 to determine the amount; or a) la somme à laquelle le requérant a droit, elle peut ordonner l’instruction de cette question ou rendre un jugement sommaire assorti d’un renvoi pour détermination de la somme conformément à la règle 153; (b) a question of law, the Court may determine the question and grant summary judgment accordingly.

propositions.text: Rule 215(3) allows summary trial or dismissal of motion if genuine issue of fact or law exists.
propositions.quote: (3) If the Court is satisfied that there is a genuine issue of fact or law for trial with respect to a claim or a defence, the Court may (3) Si la Cour est convaincue qu’il existe une véritable question de fait ou de droit litigieuse à l’égard d’une déclaration ou d’une défense, elle peut : (a) nevertheless determine that issue by way of summary trial and make any order necessary for the conduct of the summary trial; or a) néanmoins trancher cette question par voie de procès sommaire et rendre toute ordonnance nécessaire pour le déroulement de ce procès; (b) dismiss the motion in whole or in part and order that the action, or the issues in the action not disposed of by summary judgment, proceed to trial or that the action be conducted as a specially managed proceeding. b) rejeter la requête en tout ou en partie et ordonner que l’action ou toute question litigieuse non tranchée par jugement sommaire soit instruite ou que l’action se poursuive à titre d’instance à gestion spéciale.

paragraphs.summary: Rule 215 mandates summary judgment if no genuine issue exists; allows trial or summary judgment on amount or law; allows summary trial or dismissal if genuine issue exists, says the court.

propositions.text: In a motion for summary judgment each party bears the burden of putting their 'best foot forward'.
propositions.quote: According to the decision in Moroccanoil Israel Ltd. v. Lipton, 2013 FC 667, in a motion for summary judgment each party bears the burden of putting their “best foot forward”.

paragraphs.summary: The prior decision in Moroccanoil Israel Ltd. v. Lipton states each party must put their best foot forward in summary judgment motions.

propositions.text: Only the Plaintiff has filed evidence before the Court in this case.
propositions.quote: In this case, the only evidence before the Court has been filed by the Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Evidence on a motion can only be submitted by affidavit, per Rule 363.
propositions.quote: Evidence on a motion can only be submitted by way of an affidavit; see Rule 363 which provides as follows : Evidence on motion Preuve 363 A party to a motion shall set out in an affidavit any facts to be relied on by that party in the motion that do not appear on the Court file.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes only Plaintiff filed evidence, and Rule 363 requires evidence on motion be by affidavit.

propositions.text: The Defendant's statement of defence is a pleading, not evidence.
propositions.quote: The statement of defence filed by the Defendant is a pleading; it is not evidence.

propositions.text: The Defendant's oral submissions are argument, not evidence.
propositions.quote: His oral submissions are oral argument and not evidence.

propositions.text: The Defendant presented documents including an unsigned bill of sale, another bill of sale, and a bank transaction record.
propositions.quote: The documents presented by the Defendant consist of an unsigned bill of sale on a Transport Canada form, another bill of sale dated January 30, 2010 and a transaction record from the Bank of Montreal dated January 25, 2010.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Defendant's statement of defence and oral submissions are not evidence; Defendant presented some unsigned and dated documents.

propositions.text: The Defendant's documents are not attached to an affidavit and have no evidentiary value.
propositions.quote: These documents are not attached to an affidavit as exhibits. They have no present evidentiary value.

propositions.text: Only the Plaintiff's evidence is before the Court.
propositions.quote: In these circumstances, the only evidence before the Court is the evidence submitted on behalf of the Plaintiff.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Defendant's documents lack evidentiary value; only Plaintiff's evidence is before the Court.

propositions.text: The burden of proof is the civil balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The burden of proof in this matter is the civil burden of proof on the balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the burden of proof is the civil balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: The first question is whether a genuine issue for trial arises about Defendant's ownership of the Involved Ship.
propositions.quote: The first question is whether a genuine issue for trial arises with respect to the Defendant’s ownership of the Involved Ship.

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies the first issue: whether a genuine trial issue exists on Defendant's ownership of the ship.

propositions.text: No evidence from Defendant answers the claim he owns the Involved Ship under the Act or BC.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence from the Defendant to answer the claim that he is the owner of the Involved Ship, whether pursuant to the Act or under the BC.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Defendant provided no evidence disputing ownership claim under the Act or BC.

propositions.text: Section 91 of the Act defines 'owner' with reference to the Civil Liability and Bunkers Conventions or as the person with rights of possession and use.
propositions.quote: Section 91 of the Act defines “owner” as follows: owner propriétaire (a) in relation to a ship subject to the Civil Liability Convention, has the same meaning as in Article I of that Convention; ... (c) in relation to any other ship, means the person who has for the time being, either by law or by contract, the rights of the owner of the ship with respect to its possession and use.

paragraphs.summary: Section 91 of the Act defines 'owner' by reference to conventions or as person with rights of possession and use.

propositions.text: The Defendant argues he was not the owner of the Involved Ship at the time of the spill and clean-up.
propositions.quote: The Defendant argued that he was not the owner of the Involved Ship at the time of the spill and clean-up.

paragraphs.summary: The Defendant argues he was not the owner at the time of the spill and clean-up.

propositions.text: Plaintiff relies on transcripts of registry to plead Defendant is owner for this motion.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the Plaintiff relies on the transcripts of registry to plead that the Defendant is the “owner” of the Involved Ship for the purposes of this motion.

propositions.text: The question is whether a genuine issue for trial arises about ownership of the 'RYAN ATLANTIC II'.
propositions.quote: The question is whether there is a genuine issue for trial arising in respect of ownership of the “RYAN ATLANTIC II”.

paragraphs.summary: Plaintiff relies on registry transcripts to claim Defendant's ownership; Court asks if genuine trial issue exists on ownership.

propositions.text: The Canadian Register of Vessels is established under section 43 of the Canada Shipping Act, with specified duties and records.
propositions.quote: The Canadian Register of Vessels exists pursuant to section 43 of the Canada Shipping Act, S.C. 2001, c. 26, which provides as follows: Duties and powers of Chief Registrar ...

paragraphs.summary: The Canadian Register of Vessels is established under section 43 of the Canada Shipping Act with specified duties and records.

propositions.text: Despite a name spelling mistake, Plaintiff showed Defendant is owner based on registry transcripts dated December 1, 2016.
propositions.quote: In spite of the mistake in the spelling of the name on the transcript of registry dated November 4, 2014, I am satisfied that the Plaintiff has shown that the Defendant is the owner of the Involved Ship on the basis of the transcripts of registry dated December 1, 2016.

propositions.text: No genuine issue for trial arises about ownership of the involved ship.
propositions.quote: It follows that there is no genuine issue for trial arising about the ownership of the involved ship.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Plaintiff proved Defendant's ownership despite a spelling error; no genuine trial issue on ownership exists.

propositions.text: The next question is whether a genuine issue for trial arises about the amount claimed by Plaintiff.
propositions.quote: The next question is whether a genuine issue for trial arises with respect to the amount claimed by the Plaintiff.

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies the next issue: whether a genuine trial issue exists about the amount claimed by Plaintiff.

propositions.text: The Fund is created under Part 7 of the Act, authorizing CCG to respond to pollution and claim costs from the Fund.
propositions.quote: The Fund is created pursuant to Part 7 of the Act. The Act authorizes the CCG to respond to pending or actual pollution incidents and to present a claim to the Fund for repayment of the costs incurred in doing so.

paragraphs.summary: The Fund is created under the Act, authorizing CCG to respond to pollution and claim costs from the Fund.

propositions.text: Paragraphs 77(1)(a),(b) and subsection 77(2) of the Act impose liability on ship owners for pollution damage and reasonable costs.
propositions.quote: Paragraphs 77(1)(a) and (b) and subsection 77(2) of the Act are relevant and provide as follows: Liability for pollution and related costs ...

paragraphs.summary: The Act's paragraphs 77(1)(a),(b) and subsection 77(2) impose liability on ship owners for pollution damage and reasonable costs.

propositions.text: Subsection 71(a) and paragraph 71(b)(i) of the Act extend owner liability for preventive measures under the Bunkers Convention.
propositions.quote: Subsection 71(a) and paragraph 71(b)(i) of the Act are also relevant and provide as follows: Liability for pollution and related costs ...

paragraphs.summary: The Act's subsection 71(a) and paragraph 71(b)(i) extend owner liability for preventive measures under the Bunkers Convention.

propositions.text: The Defendant did not respond to the claim or challenge the amount, only denying ownership.
propositions.quote: The Defendant did not respond to the claim. In oral submissions, he did not challenge the amount but simply said that he was not the owner of the Involved Ship.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Defendant did not challenge the amount claimed, only denied ownership.

propositions.text: There is evidence the Administrator considered $358,117.79 plus $24,235.54 interest reasonable for the March 2014 incident.
propositions.quote: There is evidence before me that the Administrator considered the amount of $358,117.79 to be reasonable, in respect of the March 2014 incident, together with interest in the amount of $24, 235.54.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes evidence Administrator considered $358,117.79 plus interest reasonable for the March 2014 incident.

propositions.text: The Act mandates the Court to assess reasonableness of amounts paid by Plaintiff.
propositions.quote: The Act mandates the Court to assess the reasonableness of the amounts paid out by the Plaintiff.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the Act requires it to assess reasonableness of amounts paid by Plaintiff.

propositions.text: Defendant provided no evidence opposing amounts claimed and did not cross-examine Plaintiff's witness or exhibits.
propositions.quote: The Defendant did not provide any evidence to oppose the amounts claimed by the Plaintiff. He did not cross-examine Ms. Legars nor question any of the exhibits attached to her affidavit, including invoices.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Defendant provided no evidence opposing amounts and did not cross-examine Plaintiff's witness or exhibits.

propositions.text: The Plaintiff has shown there is no genuine issue for trial regarding the amount claimed.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Plaintiff has shown that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect to the amount claimed

propositions.text: Summary judgment is granted in favour of the Plaintiff against the Defendant.
propositions.quote: Summary judgment is granted in favour of the Plaintiff, The Administrator of the Ship-Source Oil Pollution Fund, against the Defendant, Tracy Donald Dodds.

propositions.text: The Defendant shall pay damages of $382,353.33 plus pre-judgment interest of $12,426.48, totaling $394,779.81.
propositions.quote: The Defendant, Tracy Donald Dodds, shall forthwith pay to the Plaintiff... damages in the amount of $382.353.33, plus pre-judgment interest in the amount of $12,426.48, for a total sum of $394,779.81.

propositions.text: The Plaintiff may make brief submissions on costs by February 28, 2019.
propositions.quote: The Plaintiff shall be at liberty to make brief submissions on costs by February 28, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no genuine issue for trial on the amount claimed and grants summary judgment for the Plaintiff, ordering the Defendant to pay damages and interest, with costs submissions allowed.
